clue.text: Chinese philosopher abandoning UN for His Imperial Highness's pet

indicators.note: the philosopher's name gives up these letters, with 'for' saying what takes their place

parts.note: Sun Tzu, the ancient Chinese strategist and author of The Art of War
taken as written
HIH is the standard abbreviation for His Imperial Highness

explanation.surface: An ancient Chinese thinker is set aside in favour of an emperor's lapdog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoning UN for' swaps the UN in SUNTZU for HIH, giving S + HIH + TZU.
explanation.definitionFit: The shih-tzu is a small long-haired dog breed from China, kept as a companion animal.

clue.text: Putridchapter removed by doubter

indicators.note: the doubter's word has a letter taken away from it, so this signals a deletion

parts.note: a sceptic is someone who doubts

explanation.surface: A rotten section of a book is cut out by someone sceptical of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A septic wound is infected and festering, so rotten or putrid.

clue.text: One helping to pen introductions to reprints, including The Trial

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, so the ration word wraps around the initials

parts.note: a helping or portion of food is a ration

indicators.note: the introductions to these words are their opening letters

explanation.surface: A literary assistant writes prefaces to new editions, among them Kafka's The Trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to pen' puts the three initials inside the helping after its first letter. 'The Trial' looks like Kafka's novel, but 'Trial' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial in the sense of a nuisance or vexation is something that causes annoyance.

clue.text: War story from scripture covering some medals

indicators.note: the scripture phrase covers, so it wraps around the medals

parts.note: scripture is often called the Word, here THE WORD
silvers are medals for second place

explanation.surface: A tale of war drawn from the Bible, illustrated with a few decorations.
explanation.walkthrough: The scripture phrase splits between its two words to hold the medals.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian Serraillier's children's novel follows refugee children across Europe in the Second World War.

clue.text: Wildmutualfeature of Dürrenmatt

indicators.note: wild suggests something out of control, so the letters of the next word run amok

explanation.surface: An unruly shared trait in the work of a Swiss playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: MUTUAL rearranged gives the answer. Dürrenmatt, a Swiss dramatist, carries two dots over its u.
explanation.definitionFit: The two dots over the u in the name are the diacritic mark used in German spelling.

clue.text: Journeyman asks somebody on the outside to act up

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the whole string is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to sue is to ask or petition, so asks gives sues

indicators.note: the outside of the word somebody is its first and last letters

parts.note: to act is to do

explanation.surface: A labourer begs someone outside to start misbehaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns the whole string round, as a down answer is read bottom to top. Odysseus is Homer's wanderer.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's hero spends ten years wandering home from Troy, the archetypal traveller.

clue.text: What helps footballer keep up education, mostly

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all of the word, so its final letter goes

parts.note: study is education or learning

explanation.surface: Something that helps a player stay on top of their schooling, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keep up' reads as keeping up with lessons, but it means staying upright on the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Studs on football boots grip the turf so the player does not slip over.

clue.text: Lawless fringe in penetrating MacLaverty novel

indicators.note: penetrating means getting inside, so the first pieces go into the novel's title

parts.note: Cal is a 1983 novel by Northern Irish writer Bernard MacLaverty
a rim is an edge or fringe
taken as written

explanation.surface: An unruly edge breaking into a Bernard MacLaverty book.
explanation.definitionFit: Criminal behaviour is that which breaks the law.

clue.text: Party leaderhad strugglesinbusiness

indicators.note: in means the scrambled letters sit inside the business word

parts.note: a matter is a piece of business or affair

indicators.note: struggles suggests thrashing about, so the letters of had are jumbled

explanation.surface: A political leader had a hard time at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'struggles' jumbles the three letters, and 'in' puts them into the business word after its second letter. The party is Alice in Wonderland's tea party, not a political one.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's hatter presides over the mad tea party in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

clue.text: Banker's tale confused company cashier

indicators.note: confused suggests muddled, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A muddled clerk at a firm tells a story about a bank.
explanation.walkthrough: The banker is Patrick Bateman, the investment banker narrator of Bret Easton Ellis's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Bret Easton Ellis's novel is narrated by a Wall Street investment banker who kills people.

clue.text: Baroque composer turned up with Catholic measure

indicators.note: turned means the following little word is flipped round

parts.note: RC is the abbreviation for Roman Catholic
an ell is an old measure of cloth length

explanation.surface: An early composer comes back into fashion with a devout yardstick.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Purcell was the leading English composer of the Baroque era.

clue.text: Alexander McCall Smithinitially dreamt about Booker prize success

indicators.note: initially means the opening letter of each of the novelist's names
about suggests moving around, so the letters of dreamt are mixed up

explanation.surface: A Scottish novelist first imagined winning the Booker.
explanation.walkthrough: AMS from the initials, then 'about' turns DREAMT into TERDAM. The novelist is a red herring: the winner was Ian McEwan.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian McEwan's novel won the Booker Prize in 1998.

clue.text: Web designer from city in North Carolina

definitions.meaning: the spider in E. B. White's children's book who spins words into her web
the largest city in that US state

explanation.surface: An internet designer hailing from a southern American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Web designer' suggests websites; it is the spider in E. B. White's children's book.
explanation.definitionFit: The spider of White's book shares her name with the largest city of North Carolina.

clue.text: Playwright is mingling with Jonson

indicators.note: mingling means mixing together, so the two pieces are blended into a new order

parts.note: Ben Jonson, the Jacobean playwright, so Jonson gives his first name

explanation.surface: One dramatist socialises with another, Ben Jonson.
explanation.walkthrough: IS and BEN are rearranged together to give the Norwegian dramatist.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian dramatist behind A Doll's House and Hedda Gabler.

clue.text: Nobel laureate's broadcast including everything about blue novel

indicators.note: including means the broadcast word holds the rest inside it

parts.note: to broadcast seed is to sow it

indicators.note: about means the everything word goes around the jumbled letters

parts.note: all is everything

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters of blue are given a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A prizewinner's broadcast covers a gloomy book in full.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' turns BLUE into ULBE; 'about' puts it in ALL, and 'including' puts that in SOW: S + A ULBE LL + OW.
explanation.definitionFit: The American novelist won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1976.

clue.text: People's leaderforLe Carré's emotional text?

definitions.meaning: George Smiley heads the title of Le Carré's novel ... People
emoticons in text messages, little faces showing feelings

explanation.surface: A populist figurehead stands in for a spy novelist's moving message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'People's leader' is read as the word that leads 'People' in the title Smiley's People.
explanation.definitionFit: Smiley faces are emoticons used in messages to convey mood.

clue.text: Carpenter's way ahead of kid, claiming record

indicators.note: ahead of puts the way piece before the rest in a down answer

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

indicators.note: claiming means taking in, so the kid word holds the record inside it

parts.note: to kid is to josh or tease
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A craftsman's route leads before a youngster who has a disc.
explanation.walkthrough: JOSH takes in EP to make JOSEPH, after ST, as in the abbreviation for saint.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph, husband of Mary in the Gospels, worked as a carpenter.

clue.text: Plenty of cast love to interrupt boy

parts.note: to cast off skin or leaves is to shed it

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break in, so the love letter goes into the boy word

parts.note: a lad is a boy
love is zero in tennis, written O

explanation.surface: A whole cast of actors breaks into a boy's love scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A shedload is British slang for a large amount.

clue.text: Bach's bird almost fit into market

indicators.note: into means the shortened fit word goes inside the market word

parts.note: to market goods is to sell them

indicators.note: almost means the word falls one letter short, losing its last

parts.note: an ague is a fit of shivering fever

explanation.surface: A composer's bird nearly has a seizure at a market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bach' suggests the composer; it is Richard Bach, author of Jonathan Livingston Seagull.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Bach's novella Jonathan Livingston Seagull is about a gull learning to fly.

clue.text: Architect and crime writer releasing personal scent

indicators.note: releasing means letting go of, so the scent letters drop out

parts.note: Jo Nesbo is the Norwegian crime novelist
BO stands for body odour

explanation.surface: A building designer and a thriller author give off a smell.
explanation.walkthrough: Inigo Jones was the 17th-century English architect of the Banqueting House.
explanation.definitionFit: Inigo Jones designed the Queen's House at Greenwich and Banqueting House in Whitehall.

clue.text: Horribly base place,like Shawshank?

indicators.note: horribly suggests something mangled, so the letters of the next two words are reordered

explanation.surface: A vile low dive, rather like the prison in a famous film.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the film's prison proved breakable, since Andy Dufresne got out.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Shawshank Redemption the hero gets out of the prison, so it was a place one could flee.

clue.text: Notes openings for Edith Wharton nut

parts.note: banknotes are cash

indicators.note: the openings for the novelist's names are their initial letters

explanation.surface: Banknotes start off an American novelist's nutty phase.
explanation.definitionFit: The cashew is a kidney-shaped edible seed eaten as a nut.

clue.text: Germ spread by Romeo briefly

indicators.note: spread means scattered about, so the pieces are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the name loses its final letter

explanation.surface: An infection passed on by Shakespeare's lover in short order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' clips ROMEO to ROME; 'spread' then rearranges BY + ROME.
explanation.definitionFit: A germ in the sense of a seed or bud is the early beginning from which something grows.

clue.text: Dramatic pioneer caught cutting Sachar novel after bribe

indicators.note: after places the novel-and-catch piece behind the bribe word

parts.note: a sop is a bribe offered to pacify

indicators.note: cutting means slicing into, so the cricket letter goes inside the title

parts.note: Holes is a children's novel by Louis Sachar
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Bribery follows the dismissal of a Louis Sachar book in a dramatic first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cutting' splits the novel's title after its second letter to admit the catch; 'after' puts all that behind the bribe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek tragedian helped shape early drama, adding a third actor to the stage.

clue.text: Wodehouse's choice

definitions.meaning: P. G. Wodehouse's family nickname, so his own name for himself
choice as an adjective, meaning the best, as in a choice job

explanation.walkthrough: P. G. Wodehouse was known to friends as Plum.
explanation.definitionFit: A plum job is a choice one; and it was the English humorist's nickname.

clue.text: Catch-22 creatordroppingline for Cork's outside theatre critic?

indicators.note: dropping means the line letter is let go, with for saying what replaces it

parts.note: Joseph Heller wrote the novel Catch-22

indicators.note: the outside of the city's name is its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A novelist swaps a line about an Irish city for a theatre review.
explanation.walkthrough: One L in HELLER becomes CK, the first and last letters of Cork. The question mark: a heckler criticises from the audience, not in print.
explanation.definitionFit: A heckler shouts disparaging remarks at a performer, a kind of rough audience reviewer.

clue.text: Treat Ezra with soap?

parts.note: Ezra Pound, the American modernist poet
soap comes in a cake, a solid block

explanation.surface: A poet named Ezra, given a bar of soap, takes it as a treat.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet plus a bar of soap give a rich sweet loaf.
explanation.definitionFit: A rich sponge made with butter, sugar, eggs and flour is a sweet indulgence.

clue.text: Tautology in life stories

definitions.meaning: the phrase repeats one word, saying the same thing twice
a reference book of short biographies of notable people

explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word makes the phrase look like needless repetition.
explanation.definitionFit: The annual reference book lists biographies of prominent living people.
